doc.title: George Shearing interviewed by Joe Williams, New York City, New York, March 8, 1996

title: Ellington and Strayhorn, and letting each musician contribute
summary: Shearing asks about separating Duke and Strayhorn; Williams recalls Ellington and Tom Whaley, and both note Ellington and Basie let players bring their own voice.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Can you separate Duke and Strayhorn? Who wrote what? And can you tell by listening? © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
Sometimes. But I have to sit and listen. I have to really listen.
They truly are an extension of each other, aren’t they? Ellington and Strayhorn?
That’s such a happy, happy, happy union.

I think he wanted to be like that, you know, with Tom Whaley, who also was a wonderful musician. You’d hear Duke tell him what he was going to do, and that was an experience, to hear him tell Tom Whaley, “well here, do our thing here and you know, B natural thing here, and you know, run this thing down, you know what we do, do our thing here.” And he’d say, “Oh I know what you mean.” Anybody else — Jimmie Jones is there, and Strayhorn was there, and said what the heck are they talking about?

You know, a philosophy that Duke had, I always found very interesting. You’d get a new man in the band and he would very rarely ask that man to play like so-and-so and so-and- so. He says “I don’t want that. I want that man to contribute what he has to contribute.”

There you go. That was Ellington, that was Basie. Basie had more people come through there, and it was whatever you had to contribute. That was what I was telling Leslie a while ago. I said Basie chose “Alright, O.K., You Win.” Everything else in that repertoire I chose to do. I’d have to fight him to be able to do it somewhat, because he’d say “oh you don’t need that, just do what you’re doing.”
